summary: Describes the graphics equipment at NASA's Ames Research Center in 1971, such as plotters, storage-tube displays and an IBM 2250, with more devices planned. Because the devices were so varied, Ames was building a device-independent package. It answers a request that sites describe their graphics environments.

eli5.summary: A list of every drawing machine in one lab, from pen plotters to screens. Since each speaks its own language, they were building one shared language to talk to them all.

subtitle: Graphics equipment and device-independent software at NASA Ames

tldr.problem: NASA Ames had a variety of graphics equipment (plotters, storage-tube displays, refresh CRTs) with different capabilities and interfaces, making it hard for software to use them.
tldr.mechanism: Build a device-independent graphics package that converts an intermediate language description of a picture into commands for each specific device.
tldr.outcome: One graphics program can work on many different devices, and the package can support storage of subpictures and transmission of graphics data across the network.

today: RFC 126 describes an early approach to device abstraction in graphics software. The principle of using an intermediate representation to support multiple output devices remains fundamental in graphics systems today.

sections.title: Graphics Hardware at Ames
sections.content:
As of 1971, NASA Ames Research Center for the IBM 360/67 TSS system had five graphics devices: an SC 4020 off-line microfilm system, Calcomp plotters, ARDS storage-tube CRTs, IMLAC PDS-1 refresh CRTs, and one IBM 2250 CRT. Additional devices were planned, including an Evans and Sutherland LDS-2 system and Hazeltine alphanumeric CRTs.

This diverse collection presented a software engineering challenge: each device had different capabilities and expected different command formats.
sections.eli5: The lab had many different drawing machines: some that printed on paper, some that drew on film, some that showed pictures on screens. Each one spoke its own language.

sections.title: Device-Independent Graphics
sections.content:
Rather than writing separate code for each device, Ames developed a device-independent graphics package. The core uses a device-independent intermediate language that describes a picture in abstract terms, without reference to any specific hardware. When a device is selected, a conversion step translates the intermediate language into the specific commands that device understands.

The package also provides features for defining and storing subpictures, which can be reused in constructing more complex pictures. Graphics data sets can be transmitted across the TSS network to other installations, allowing shared work on graphics.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a different program for each machine, they write one program that describes pictures in a universal language. Another program translates that language to whatever machine is being used.

sections.title: Network Graphics and Scaling
sections.content: RFC 126 notes that ILLIAC IV would become a functioning node at Ames in the future, and the author asks other sites to describe their graphics environments and their plans for using graphics with ILLIAC IV. This indicates that graphics capabilities were expected to be shared and used across the network.
sections.eli5: As the network grows, different laboratories will want to share their graphics work. The device-independent approach makes that possible.
